passage: In the school library in Auckland, Mateo, Mei and a third friend stared at a whiteboard covered in ideas: accounts, star ratings, comments, a forum, dark mode. “We have four weeks and one laptop,” Mei said. “What does someone need on day one?” Mateo thought aloud. “A student wants last year's notes. That's all. One page, PDFs sorted by subject.” “No login?” “No login. If people use it, we add ratings later. If nobody does, at least we didn't build a forum for no one.” Mei rubbed out every item except PDFs by subject and drew a box round it. By Friday they had uploaded twelve files into six folders, and the whole site fit on one page.

qa.q: How many files did the group upload by Friday?
What might Mei be feeling as Mei rubs out the list?
qa.a: Relieved and focused: the smaller target makes the four weeks look manageable.

qa.q: What else could the group do to decide what to add next, and why?
qa.a: Ask classmates what they miss after using the first version, since real users show which extras matter.

qa.q: How does the plan look to a student who just wants last year's notes?
qa.a: That student gets what they need straight away and does not care about ratings or a forum yet.

grounding: A group decides that the first version of a notes site is just uploaded PDFs sorted by subject, leaving accounts and ratings for later.

passage:
In the student council room after school, the whiteboard was already full: logins, star ratings, comments, a dark theme, a search bar. Sarika capped the marker.
“Okay, stop. If we build all this, when do we launch?”
Asif counted on his fingers. “Maybe March?”
“And pre-boards are in January. The people who need notes need them before that.” She wiped half the board. “So what's the smallest thing that's still useful? Someone from Class Ten opens a page, clicks Chemistry, gets the PDFs. That's it.”
“No logins? Then anyone could upload rubbish.”
“So for now only we upload. People send us their notes, we check them and put them up.”
Asif frowned, then wrote VERSION 1 at the top: one page, PDFs under each subject. Below a line, smaller: Later: accounts, ratings.
“We could have that up by next Friday,” he said.

qa.q: When are the pre-boards, according to Sarika?
Why does Sarika cap the marker and say "stop"?
qa.a: She is worried the long feature list will push the launch past the pre-boards, and feels impatient to get something useful to students first.

qa.q: What else could help the team decide what goes into version one?
qa.a: Asking a few Class Ten students what they need most, so the first page matches real demand rather than guesses.

qa.q: How might a Class Ten student looking for notes see this plan?
qa.a: They get chemistry PDFs before pre-boards without signing up, which matters far more to them than ratings.

grounding: Shows a student team reasoning that version one of a notes site is just one page of PDFs by subject, with accounts and ratings left for later.

passage:
Hi Kashish,
I've been thinking about Saturday's meeting, and I want to argue for something before we start building. Please read to the end before replying!
Our list has twelve features. Your login page design looks great, honestly. But if we build all twelve, the notes site will be ready after the exams it's meant for. So I asked myself: what is the least we can put online that still helps someone on Monday? My answer is one page with subject headings (Physics, Chemistry, Maths, Biology) and the PDFs people have already shared with us listed under each. No accounts, no ratings, no comments.
Then we watch. If people use it and ask for logins, your design goes in next. If nobody opens it, we've lost a week, not a term.
Can we talk about this at lunch tomorrow?
Tushar

qa.q: How many features are on the team's list?
What might Tushar be worried about while writing this email?
qa.a: Tushar is worried the site will be ready only after the exams, and seems a little anxious about disappointing Kashish by setting the login design aside.

qa.q: What would make Tushar's case stronger at lunch?
qa.a: A rough sketch of the single page and a couple of classmates' requests for notes, so the idea is concrete and tied to real need.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel reading that the login page is set aside?
qa.a: Kashish may feel a pang of disappointment, but also reassured, since the email praises the design and promises it comes next if people ask.

grounding: Shows a teen reasoning that version one of a notes site should be a single page of PDFs by subject, with accounts and ratings saved for later.
